political_impact.text: Apart from the fine-arts council, the January 1909 orders, including the Pelican Island enlargement, passed without national comment.

reception.text: The Council of the Fine Arts drew respectful notice from the architectural and artistic professions.

political_impact.text: The council met on February 9, 1909, and approved the Senate Park Commission's site for the Lincoln Memorial; McKim, very ill, attended briefly and later resigned, and Burnham was absent.
political_impact.source: Kohler, "The Commission of Fine Arts: Implementing the Senate Park Commission's Vision," U.S. Commission of Fine Arts

political_impact.text: Representative John J. Fitzgerald of New York moved to bar payment to members of the "so-called Council of Fine Arts," saying its duty should be fixed by Congress and not by the Executive; the amendment carried on a division, 67 to 17.
political_impact.source: Congressional Record, 60th Cong., 2d sess., vol. 43, pp. 2918–2922

political_impact.text: The sundry civil act struck at the council twice: a proviso barred paying its members or spending on plans it had approved, and section 9 barred paying any commission or council not authorized by law.
political_impact.source: Act of March 4, 1909, ch. 299, 35 Stat. 945, at 959 and 1027

political_impact.text: The fight came amid a wider clash between Congress and Roosevelt over commissions it had not authorized, including the Keep, Inland Waterways, National Conservation and Country Life commissions.

legacy.text: Congress created a permanent Commission of Fine Arts of seven members in 1910; it still reviews the design of monuments, memorials and buildings in the capital and traces its lineage to the 1909 council.
The statutory commission's seats were written to include distinguished laymen, where all thirty of Roosevelt's appointees had been practicing artists and designers.

today.name: U.S. Commission of Fine Arts
today.note: Created by statute in 1910; traces its lineage to the 1909 council.

later_actions.text: The sundry civil appropriation act cut off funds for the council by name and under a general ban on unauthorized commissions.
President Taft revoked the order by Executive Order 1074, citing the sundry civil act of March 4, 1909.
Congress created the Commission of Fine Arts by statute.

legacy.text: Proclamation 2416 renamed the reservation Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge in 1940.
Most of the modern refuge's 5,376 acres was acquired after 1968.

today.name: Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: The mangrove islands added in 1909 enlarged the first federal bird reservation.

related.note: The original 1903 Pelican Island order, which this order enlarged; it dates that order to March 13, 1903, where contemporary records give March 14.

later_actions.text: Renamed Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge by Proclamation 2416.

uncertain: How many acres the 1909 enlargement added is not known; only the diagram attached to the signed order at the National Archives could settle it, and Palmer's 1912 figure of 5.50 acres may or may not include the 1909 islands.
